terms.meaning: units of size: a MiB is 1024 times 1024 bytes, and a GiB is 1024 MiB
the ending of a file name, such as xml or zip
an optional extra document uploaded with the schedule

sections.name: File setup, SCHEDULE_SUFFIXES, FileIdentity, FileValidation, InputKind
sections.title: Upload limits and accepted types
sections.what: Sets the maximum sizes for schedules, single attachments and all attachments, and lists the schedule file endings the app accepts.
sections.why: Keeps the limits and accepted types in one place.
sections.watch_out: These values must match the server's limits, or users will see messages that disagree with what the server accepts.

sections.name: validatePackage
sections.title: Check for a project package
sections.what: Checks a ZIP project package: it must end in zip, not be empty, and not exceed the 512 MiB limit. It tells the user the next step, but it does not look inside the archive.
sections.why: Packages are a separate upload mode with their own rules.
sections.watch_out: Archive contents are only checked on the server, so this check says the file is accepted for upload, not that the content is valid.

sections.name: formatBytes
sections.title: Human-readable file size
sections.what: Turns a number of bytes into text such as bytes, KiB, MiB or GiB, choosing the unit by size.
sections.why: Users see sizes in the messages, so they should be easy to read.
sections.watch_out: The unit labels are binary sizes but the rounding is simple, so very near a boundary the displayed size can look slightly off.

sections.name: validateSchedule
sections.title: Check for a schedule file
sections.what: Checks a schedule file: a ZIP is refused with a pointer to package mode, BIM model types are refused with an explanation, other unknown types are refused, and empty or oversized files are refused.
sections.why: Gives the user a specific reason for each refusal, so they know what to do next.
sections.watch_out: BIM model files are refused because import is not built yet. The message makes clear that IFC export is a different feature.

sections.name: validateAttachments
sections.title: Check optional attachments
sections.what: Checks each optional attachment is not empty and is within 512 MiB, and that all attachments together are within 1 GiB. Any document type is accepted.
sections.why: Optional documents are kept for later review even when the app cannot read them.
sections.watch_out: Because all types are accepted, an unreadable file will not be flagged here. It will be kept for review.

sections.name: validateRefinementAttachments
sections.title: Check files for evidence refinement
sections.what: Applies tighter rules for evidence refinement: at most 10 files, 50 MiB each, 100 MiB in total, then the normal attachment checks.
sections.why: Refinement runs on smaller batches than the first upload.
sections.watch_out: These limits are typed directly into the function, not in the constants at the top, so a limit change could be missed.

summary: Checks the files a user picks before upload: the file name ending, whether the file is empty, and whether it is too large. Each check returns a plain message the user can act on.
purpose: Gives the user a clear reason before a large upload is attempted.
why: Reason not stated in the code. Likely reason: catching problems early avoids sending files the server would reject.
how: Each validation function first checks the file name ending, then emptiness, then the size limit, and returns a message. The attachment check adds up the total size of all optional files.
inputs: Lists of file names and sizes, one file at a time, plus the optional attachment list.
outputs: A valid flag with a message for schedules and packages, a message or nothing for attachments, and a readable size text.
risks: Checks use the file name and size only, not the contents. The real check happens on the server, so a bad file can pass here.
debug: If a valid file is rejected, check the file name ending and the limit constants at the top. If a message looks wrong, check the matching function.
